task: What does a valid WebMCP Challenge submission have to include? List all deliverables and the specific requirements for the project description, demo video, and source-code repository.
answer:
A valid submission must include: (1) a project built with the required WebMCP developer tools that meets the Project Requirements; (2) a working live URL accessible to judges in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or in WebMCP-enabled Chrome (hosting provider is unrestricted, and authenticated apps may supply credentials in the Submission Form); (3) a text description; (4) a public source-code repository URL; and (5) a demonstration video.

The text description must explain why the use case strongly fits WebMCP, how it creates a better user experience, what people and agents can do together that was previously difficult or impossible, and briefly how WebMCP was implemented.

The public repository must be on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket; contain all source code, assets, and instructions needed to make the project functional; expose the WebMCP tool registration (the rules illustrate document.modelContext.registerTool); and be open source, with an open-source license file detectable and visible at the top of the repository page/About section.

The demo video must be under three minutes (judges need not watch past three minutes), clearly show the project functioning, include audio explaining what was built and how WebMCP was used, be uploaded publicly to YouTube with its link entered on the submission form, and contain no third-party trademarks, copyrighted music, or other copyrighted material unless permission was obtained.

task: Can a project begun before August 25, 2026 qualify? Explain which work counts, how judges assess it, and what evidence the entrant must provide.
answer: Yes. A project that existed before August 25, 2026 can qualify, but it must be meaningfully extended with WebMCP after the Submission Period began (August 25 at 11:00 a.m. PT). For a pre-existing project, judges evaluate only the work added during the Submission Period—not the earlier project as a whole. The entrant must clearly separate prior work from new work and provide evidence that the WebMCP extension occurred during the Submission Period, such as timestamped/dated commit history or equivalent documentation.

task: Give the final extended submission deadline in PT and in EDT. Explain why it changed and identify the three project artifacts that must remain unchanged after submissions close.
answer: The final extended deadline is Friday, September 4, 2026 at 1:00 a.m. PT, which is 4:00 a.m. EDT. It moved by 12 hours because an ongoing outage was affecting entrants while the OpenAI team worked on a fix. After submissions close, the three artifacts that must stay unchanged are the source-code repository, the demo video, and the live application/site: do not edit the repo, replace the video, change the live site, or take that site offline.

task: How do the two judging stages work? Name all four equally weighted criteria in the second stage and explain the tie-breaking order.
answer:
Stage One is a pass/fail viability screen: the project must reasonably fit the hackathon theme and reasonably apply the required featured APIs/SDKs. Every submission that passes proceeds to Stage Two, where judges score four equally weighted criteria: WebMCP Leverage (thorough, skillful, genuinely effortful, working and non-trivial WebMCP use); Execution (a working/runnable, complete and coherent product experience, not merely a technical proof of concept); Potential Impact (a credible, specific real problem and audience, with the demonstrated solution actually addressing it); and Creativity & Ambition (novelty, creativity, ambition, and differentiation from existing concepts).

For a tie, compare the tied entries on the criteria in their listed order: first WebMCP Leverage, then Execution, then Potential Impact, then Creativity & Ambition, stopping when one has the higher score. If they remain tied on every criterion, the judging panel votes.

task: How can judges test a submitted application in each supported browser environment? Include the minimum Chrome version and required flag, whether judges must open the live application, and where an entrant must provide private login credentials.
answer: Judges can test in either supported environment. In the ChatGPT desktop app, they use the in-app browser, where WebMCP support is enabled by default, and open the submitted working live URL. In Google Chrome, they need Chrome 149 or later, must enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, restart Chrome, and then open the submitted live application with WebMCP enabled. So yes: the entrant must provide an accessible working live URL (or qualifying website/functioning demo/test build), and judges test the actual live application rather than only reviewing its description or video. If the app/site is private, login credentials must be included in the submission’s testing instructions; the rules also say authenticated-app credentials can be added on the Submission Form.
